revisions.body: The frame makes Socrates’ return a change of register: from a campaign just marked by the deaths of acquaintances to the familiar palestra and its talk of philosophy and promising young men. One way to read the setting is as a juxtaposition of public danger with the social world into which Socrates reenters—and of the questions this community chooses to pursue.

The turn is not from a passive Socrates to an active one: he has already initiated the question about philosophy and the young men at 153d. Here, after Chaerephon prompts him about Charmides’ face, Socrates redirects the shared admiration toward the soul. He accepts the language of beauty, then proposes examining whether Charmides is well-formed in soul and calls for conversation. The philosophical procedure grows out of the spectacle rather than simply replacing it.

Charmides’ arrival unsettles the confidence Socrates expected to bring to the conversation. He reports being thrown into aporia, losing his former boldness, catching fire, and imagining himself as prey in Cydias’ fawn-and-lion image. I would not turn that erotic disturbance into a diagnosis that he has lost sophrosyne. The narrower irony is sharper: the speaker presenting a cure is himself unable to command his response to the encounter.

Socrates turns the promised cure into a conditional test: if Charmides already has sophrosyne, the remedy can be given directly; if not, the incantation comes first. The therapeutic sequence therefore identifies the immediate question of the inquiry—not yet a definition, but whether the quality is present at all.

Socrates proceeds on a premise worth noticing: if temperance is present, Charmides should have some perception and opinion of it, and should be able to say what it is. The passage thus treats possession as a possible route to articulation. Whether that route will hold remains open; for now, it is the test placed before Charmides.

At 160a–160b, Socrates’ questions keep moving while Charmides’ replies contract into brief confirmations: “true,” “yes,” “that is so,” and “it looks like it.” This compressed response pattern lets Socrates carry the argument from quick understanding and deliberation to a general claim about soul and body before stating the consequence for quietness. The exchange gives Socrates the argumentative momentum without requiring us to decide that Charmides is insincere.

Charmides’ concession closes this test, and Socrates immediately gives the inquiry a new instruction: look into yourself, consider what temperance does to you when present, and infer what sort of thing could produce that effect. The passage clearly requests self-examination. Whether this marks a genuine change of method or simply frames the next attempt is left open; what matters here is the restart.

Socrates tests Critias’s proposal by adding a condition about awareness. The doctor may produce a benefit, but Socrates asks whether the doctor must know when the treatment helps rather than harms. Critias answers, “perhaps not.” The important pressure point is not simply whether the doctor performs a good act; it is whether the agent’s knowledge must include the value of that act. One way to read the exchange is as a shift from judging results to examining self-knowledge.

Critias refuses the implication that someone could be temperate without knowing it: if that follows from his earlier admissions, he would retract those admissions rather than accept the result. He then recasts temperance as self-knowledge and invokes the Delphic inscription in support, reading its wording as a riddling divine address rather than an ordinary greeting. One way to hear the move is as a shift from defending the earlier premises to offering a new definition and a reason for it.

Socrates asks Critias to identify both the subject and the product of temperance, using medicine and building as immediate examples. Critias objects that self-knowledge is unlike the other sciences and points out that calculation and geometry do not yield tangible products like houses or cloaks. Socrates accepts the objection, then changes the question: instead of asking for a product, he asks what each science is about, illustrating the new approach with the even and odd, and with the heavy and light. The pressure shifts from output to object.

At 166c Critias says that Socrates is trying to refute him while leaving the subject of the discussion behind. Socrates answers that he is examining the argument because he fears mistaking ignorance for knowledge, and asks Critias to attend to what the argument itself will show. Critias then states that temperance is knowledge of itself and of the other sciences; Socrates immediately asks whether it therefore includes knowledge of ignorance. What should we make of this exchange: does the new definition clarify the inquiry, or does the accusation of refutation remain part of the problem?

Socrates does not yet settle what a science of science can do. He grants its possibility only to keep the discussion moving, then asks whether it can distinguish anything beyond knowledge from non-knowledge. Critias answers, “No, only that.” The exchange therefore makes this a test of the proposed science’s reach, while leaving its existence itself for later examination.

The passage holds a hope and a result apart. Under the earlier, broader hypothesis, knowing what one knows and does not know would let people entrust unfamiliar tasks to those with the relevant knowledge and live without error. Socrates then states the present result: no such science has appeared, and Critias agrees. Read as an argument, the contrast keeps the promised benefit conditional rather than turning it into an established achievement.

Socrates labels the proposal a dream after admitting he may be talking nonsense, so the thought experiment arrives with its certainty deliberately lowered. Yet he asks us to grant its strongest consequence: if temperance governed as defined, ignorance could not pass itself off as expertise, and life would proceed according to knowledge. The decisive gap comes at the end. Even after granting that scenario, Socrates says they still cannot learn whether knowledgeable action makes us happy. One way to hear the passage is as a test of sufficiency: better knowledge may secure competent action without, by itself, explaining eudaimonia.

Socrates now tests the word “knowledge” by forcing it into particular crafts, beginning with shoemaking. The exchange keeps the happiness criterion unresolved rather than proving that every skilled activity makes its practitioner happy. Socrates then imagines a person who knows everything past, present, and future and asks which science makes him happy—or whether all do alike. I hear Critias’ final “not alike” as keeping that question open, not as identifying a single science. The next pressure point is therefore the missing link between knowledge and happiness.

Critias’s answer makes knowledge of good and bad the single knowledge connected with doing well and being happy, rather than merely the sum of all technical know-how. Socrates marks this shift with a personal accusation: he says Critias has been leading him in circles and concealing the answer. That is Socrates’ charge, not proof of Critias’ intention. He then tests the distinction by asking whether the other crafts would lose their own work if this knowledge were removed. They would not. The pressure point is therefore not whether each craft can perform its task, but what makes its result beneficial.

Charmides keeps the ending unresolved: he says he cannot know whether he has temperance because the inquiry has not discovered what it is, yet he is willing to keep receiving Socrates’ charm. Critias turns that willingness into a proposed test, saying it will be evidence of temperance if Charmides stays with Socrates. Read the comedy carefully: obedience satisfies the guardian’s test, but the exchange does not certify the virtue. It ends with a promise of treatment and a playful threat of force, not with temperance securely established.
